items.title: Funding timing
items.text: Earthbond’s raises coincided with Nigeria’s 2023–2024 fuel price rises, which made solar more competitive against diesel generation. It secured funding from Catalyst Fund and Madica after demonstrating proof of concept with SMEs. The sequence is consistent with milestone-based fundraising, though Earthbond’s runway before these investments is unknown.

items.title: Instrument choice
items.text: Earthbond’s disclosed financing is a grant and two small early-stage cheques; the instruments behind the Catalyst Fund and Madica investments (for example, SAFEs or priced equity) are not disclosed. It carries no disclosed debt at firm level; blended finance applies only downstream, through its lending partners.

items.title: Investor selection
items.text: Earthbond’s early backers span three types: an accelerator fund (Catalyst Fund), a fintech pre-seed programme (Madica) and a development-agency grant (develoPPP). The mix limits the equity sold, although founder ownership is not disclosed, and leaves no clear lead for a priced round.

items.title: Dilution management
items.text: Founder dilution is undisclosed. The grant is non-dilutive; whether the two investments have converted into equity is not public.

items.title: Follow-on funding and debt/equity decisions
items.text: Earthbond has no disclosed priced follow-on, but drew capital from three sources within nine months (March–December 2024), a sign of early institutional interest, though weaker than a lead investor increasing its commitment. It carries no disclosed corporate debt, relying on an embedded-finance model instead. No decision to decline or delay capital is documented.

why: Chidalu Onyenso grew up in New Jersey but stayed connected to Nigeria through annual family visits. After Princeton, she built product and market experience at IBM, Fundera and a Nairobi-based startup, then attended Harvard Business School, where she used nights and a summer grant to build Earthbond. She set out to tackle SME financing in Africa but found unreliable power to be the binding constraint, and founded Earthbond in 2022 as a solar marketplace connecting businesses to power audits, installers and credit providers. It has raised more than $400,000 in grants and venture capital, while partner microfinance banks lend and carry the credit risk.
lessons: Layering accelerator, fintech pre-seed and development-agency grant capital can fund a pre-seed company while limiting the equity sold (Earthbond’s founder ownership is not disclosed), but is sustainable only if one of these backers, or a new investor, leads the next priced round.

Keeping asset-financing risk on a banking partner’s balance sheet lets a pre-seed company reach the market without a loan book, but it cedes margin and control over credit decisions to the partner, and growth depends on the partner’s appetite to lend.
